title: Design exercise: API rate limiter
summary: A classic design exercise: rate limiting for a public API served from twenty gateway nodes, with a 1 ms decision budget and a limiter that must never become the outage. The reference answer keeps token buckets on each node, corrects them from a shared store every 100 ms, fails open by default, and bounds overshoot in numbers. Converted by hand from the module outline's reference answer and its 45-minute script; every number and source is kept.

exercise.prompt: Design the rate limiting for a public HTTP API served from many gateway nodes. Each API key has a limit; callers over the limit get a 429. The product team wants to add tiers and per-endpoint costs later.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: A per-key limit with a burst; 429 with headers that tell the caller when to retry; policies editable without a deploy.
50,000 requests per second across 20 gateway nodes in one region; 1 million active keys.
Typical limits of 100 requests per second with a burst of 200; a few keys hold 30 to 40 percent of traffic.
derive the per-node rate, the policy data size and the per-node bucket memory yourself
The decision adds under 1 ms at p99; the limiter must never make the API unavailable.
Overshoot of up to 10 percent over a one-second window is acceptable; sustained overshoot is not.
DDoS protection at the network layer, billing.

clarifying_questions.q: Per key, per user or per IP?
clarifying_questions.a: Per key; per IP is a separate abuse limiter.

clarifying_questions.q: What if the shared store is down?
clarifying_questions.a: The API must stay up; limits may loosen, and that must be visible.
Later, via a cost per request.
Per region now; a global view later.

blocks.text: The limiter is a library inside each gateway node plus a shared store, not a separate network hop, because of the latency budget. Local buckets decide; the shared store corrects them a few times per second; a policy service pushes policies that every node caches.

blocks.text: Stripe's write-up describes the token bucket with a centralised bucket host that every request consults; this answer moves the bucket into the node and keeps the shared store as a correction, which trades a little exactness for the round trip. The sliding window counter in the store is the Cloudflare method: two fixed-window counters, the previous one weighted by how much of it overlaps the sliding window.

blocks.legend: The architecture, the same boxes as the neutral diagram, one AWS service each: the load balancer is an Application Load Balancer, the 20 gateway nodes are ECS on Fargate tasks that keep the local buckets in memory, the shared counter store is an ElastiCache for Valkey cluster with a replica in another zone that takes over on failure s14, the backend services and the policy service are ECS on Fargate services, and the metrics go to CloudWatch. The policies table is the one box the neutral diagram leaves implicit, as the load balancer is; the clients and the operators reach only the load balancer. The neutral diagram's push becomes the poll. The CloudWatch alarms that the operators watch are the reader of the metrics. Tasks find the backends and the policy service through AWS Cloud Map DNS names s13; a lookup returns up to eight healthy records, which is enough for the two policy tasks and enough to spread load over the backends, and it is why no box here depends on one lookup reaching every gateway task. Policies are not pushed: each gateway task asks the policy service for anything newer than its version every 5 seconds, so an edit reaches every task within about 6 seconds (the policy service refreshes from the table once a second, then the 5 s poll), and a task that cannot reach the policy service keeps the set it has. Operators edit through the load balancer: its admin listener rule authenticates them with Amazon Cognito or an OIDC provider before forwarding s43. Calls to DynamoDB go over a gateway endpoint s18 and the metrics over an interface endpoint s19; the counter correction is one pipelined call per report s15. Sync means the caller waits for the answer; async means the work goes on after the request has been answered. The VPC frames are one VPC in one Region across three Availability Zones.

blocks.text: The request path through AWS: the decision on a gateway task, which is all the client waits for.

blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed. Edge is the Application Load Balancer, which routes only to healthy targets s12; ECS replaces a task that fails the check s11. The token take is an in-memory operation, not a call, which is how the design keeps its decision under 1 ms. A replacement task's buckets start full, the one burst of overshoot the failure table accepts. The 429 and the RateLimit headers are the contract of the neutral data model.

blocks.text: The load balancer sends a request to any healthy task, and each task decides alone from its own buckets; the counters never sit on this path. A task that fails its health check is replaced and its buckets start full, so a restart costs one burst of overshoot and no more.
The correction loop and the metrics, which run on the node's own timers.

Each report is one pipelined round trip with an INCRBY and a GET per active key s15, s16; at most 250 keys per node per report, since a node decides 2,500 times a second. A failover to the replica s14 is a window in which the call times out and the node enforces its local buckets alone. The metrics are statistic sets, one call carrying many data points s17.

blocks.text: The store being down is a loosening, not an outage: every task keeps enforcing its share, and the unreachable-store metric is what raises the alarm.
The policy path: an operator edit is written to DynamoDB by the policy service, and every gateway task polls for anything newer than its version, every 5 seconds.

the operator first Edge->>PS: HTTP, the admin path PS->>DDB: transaction: policy item, version +1 DDB-->>PS: ok PS-->>Edge: saved Edge-->>Op: saved loop every second, each policy task PS->>DDB: GetItem, the version
(a Query if it moved) DDB-->>PS: the version end loop every 5 s, each gateway task GW->>PS: GET policies newer than version N alt nothing newer PS-->>GW: 304, same version else a newer version PS-->>GW: the changed policies, version N+1 end end Note over GW: cached until the next poll opt the policy service is down Note over GW: cached policies still apply end
blocks.legend: A new task starts with an empty set and its first poll, "newer than version 0", returns the whole set; this is the policies() call of the neutral API, now the same call every 5 seconds. An edit is one transaction on the policy item and a version item, so a reader never sees a new version with old policies. The two policy tasks answer from memory and re-read the version once a second; the bound from an edit to every task is about 6 seconds, and a policy-service outage delays changes but never a decision. The policy service is found by its service discovery DNS name s13, and DynamoDB is reached over a gateway endpoint s18.

blocks.caption: Identity and network: who may call what, over which endpoint, and what is public. Only the load balancer is public: it sits in the VPC's public subnets. Every ECS service and the cache run in private subnets across three Availability Zones in awsvpc mode, one network interface per task, each service under its own IAM task role, so permissions go to the task and not to a host. A task in a private subnet pulls its image through the Amazon ECR interface endpoints and an S3 gateway endpoint, and this design uses those, not a NAT gateway.

blocks.caption: Where the per-key limit runs: your own limiter in the gateway tasks, Amazon API Gateway usage plans, or an AWS WAF rate-based rule.

rows.option: A limiter library in the gateway tasks, with a Valkey correction loop
rows.pick_when: the limit is per key with a burst at a per-second grain, the decision must cost almost nothing, and the policies, tiers and per-request costs are the product's to define
rows.avoid_when: the API is small, the keys are few, and enforcement that is only approximate is fine, so a managed feature does the job without code to run
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The limit is per key with a burst, the decision budget is a millisecond, and the shape of the policies (tiers, a cost per request) will keep changing.

rows.option: Amazon API Gateway usage plans (REST API)
rows.pick_when: a limited set of API keys, each with its own rate, burst and quota, and nobody wants to run a limiter; the token bucket is built in
rows.avoid_when: the keys number in the millions, the request rate is above the account's throttle quota, or the limits must be exact: usage plan limits are targets, applied on a best-effort basis
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. A Region holds a fixed 10,000 API keys against a million keys here, the limits are best effort where the design bounds its overshoot, and per-request billing at this rate would be the biggest line of the bill.

rows.option: An AWS WAF rate-based rule on the load balancer
rows.pick_when: the limit is per source IP or per header value, over a window of a minute or more, and a blocked request should never reach the gateway tasks
rows.avoid_when: the limit is per second with a burst, or per API key with tier policies: the shortest evaluation window is a minute and enforcement is near the limit, not exact
rows.example: For this design: not chosen for the key limit. It is the right tool for the per-IP abuse limiter that the clarifying questions set aside, and the Reliability pillar lists a missing per-IP limit as an anti-pattern.

blocks.caption: The shared counter store: ElastiCache for Valkey, DynamoDB or MemoryDB.

rows.option: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey, node-based, with a replica in another zone
rows.pick_when: the counters are small, hot and cheap to lose, and one pipelined round trip can carry the increments of many keys
rows.avoid_when: the counters are a record that must survive a node loss, such as a billed quota
rows.example: For this design: chosen. A lost window only loosens limits for one interval, a report is one round trip for all of a node's active keys, and the bill grows with nodes, not with requests.

rows.pick_when: each counter must be durable, writes touch one key at a time, and nobody wants to run a cluster
rows.avoid_when: a report must increment many counters at once: BatchWriteItem cannot update items, and a transaction is limited to 100 actions and bills every item twice, so the write count stays at one per active key
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. One write per active key per report is the same write count as the exact design's one per request, so the correction loop would save nothing on the bill.

rows.pick_when: the counters are the source of truth and must survive a node loss without a rebuild, and the Valkey commands are wanted
rows.avoid_when: the counters are a correction that the design can lose and refill
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Durable counters would be the quota system that the 10x table keeps out of the limiter; here a lost window refills within one interval.

blocks.caption: The gateway tasks and the policy service: ECS on Fargate, Lambda or EKS.

rows.pick_when: long-lived container processes that hold state in memory and run their own timers, behind a load balancer, with no cluster to patch
rows.avoid_when: the load is bursty and mostly idle, or the team already runs Kubernetes for everything else
rows.example: For this design: chosen for the gateway tasks and the policy service. Each gateway task holds its buckets in memory and runs the correction timer, on Arm tasks across three Availability Zones. The fleet is fixed at 20 tasks, so each bucket's share is a constant; a change of the count is a change of policy.

rows.pick_when: short, stateless handlers with spiky or low traffic, where paying per request beats paying for idle tasks
rows.avoid_when: a handler must keep state in memory between requests or run a timer: the execution environment is frozen after each invocation, and per-request billing at a steady high rate costs more than the tasks
rows.example: For this design: not chosen for the gateway. The local buckets and the correction timer need a process that keeps running; a function could serve the policy service's rare edits, which is not worth a second compute model.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes and needs its ecosystem (a service mesh, operators, portability across clouds)
rows.avoid_when: the workload is one fleet of identical gateway tasks and a small service; the upgrade cadence buys nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing here needs the Kubernetes API, and a cluster brings three major releases a year to track for two kinds of container.

blocks.caption: The policy store: DynamoDB, a relational database, or AWS AppConfig.

rows.pick_when: policies are read by key or pattern, the set is read in full only at start, and writes are rare
rows.avoid_when: policy administration needs joins across tiers, customers and endpoints, or ad hoc reporting
rows.example: For this design: chosen. A policy is looked up by key or pattern, and the whole set (about 100 MB) is read by the policy service and polled by the tasks.

rows.option: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL or Amazon RDS
rows.pick_when: tiers, per-endpoint costs and customers become relational data that product and support teams query and report on
rows.avoid_when: the data is a key-to-policy lookup with rare writes and no reporting
rows.example: For this design: not chosen now. When the product team adds tiers and per-endpoint costs, as the prompt says, the admin side may want a relational store; the gateway tasks would still read a pushed copy, so nothing on the request path changes.

rows.pick_when: a small configuration changes without a deploy and needs validation, a gradual rollout and automatic rollback
rows.avoid_when: the data is larger than the hosted configuration size limit
rows.example: For this design: not chosen for the policy set, which is far larger than the hosted configuration limit of 2 MB; a fit for a handful of fleet-wide switches such as the fail-open flag.

blocks.text: The messaging fork does not apply here: nothing sits in a queue. The decision is a call in the gateway process, the correction is a direct pipelined call that nothing needs to buffer, and a queue on the decision path would add the hop that the 1 ms budget does not have.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: The decision path on one node, and the correction loop behind it.

blocks.title: How each node sizes its bucket
items: Each node holds a token bucket per key sized to its share of the limit: with 20 nodes and random balancing, each node gets about 1/20 of a key's traffic, so each bucket refills at rate/20 with burst/20.

blocks.text: Part a: the decision on one node, which is all the request waits for.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as API client participant G as Gateway node participant B as Backend C->>G: request, API key Note over G: take cost tokens
from the local bucket alt the bucket has the tokens G->>B: forward the request B-->>G: response G-->>C: response, RateLimit headers else the bucket is empty G-->>C: 429, Retry-After, headers Note over G,B: no backend cost end
blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed. The 429 carries Retry-After s4 and the RateLimit headers s5; an empty bucket answers at the node, so the backend never sees the request.

blocks.text: Part b: the correction loop behind the decision, off the request path.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 6 participant G as Gateway node participant S as Shared store loop every 100 ms (assumption) G->>S: report counts per active key S-->>G: global count, last second end alt over the limit globally, allowed locally Note over G: tighten that key's
bucket for the next interval end Note over G,S: the store corrects,
it does not decide
blocks.legend: The loop is the node's own timer, not part of any request. A hot key pinned to few nodes or uneven balancing is the case the tightening step is for.

blocks.text: If the global count shows a key over its limit while the local buckets allowed it (uneven balancing, a hot key pinned to few nodes), the node tightens that key's local bucket for the next interval. The shared store therefore corrects, it does not decide; its latency is off the request path.
The store's own cost is 20 nodes times 10 reports per second, each a batch of the node's active keys, which is a few hundred batched writes per second, not 50,000 single ones.

When the shared store is slow or down, the design fails open: nodes keep enforcing local buckets at their share, so each key is still bounded (by at most the number of nodes times its share, in the worst case of all traffic for a key on one node, which balancing makes unlikely). Emit a metric and an alert the moment the store is unreachable.

Fail closed (reject when the store is unreachable) would turn a store outage into an API outage, which breaks the first target; fail closed is the right choice only where the limit protects something that must not be exceeded, such as a payment endpoint with a legal cap, and that is a per-policy flag. This follows the overload guidance of the SRE book's handling-overload chapter (reject cheaply, protect the service, never let the protection become the outage) and the Builders' Library article on load shedding, which measures the service by goodput rather than throughput.

blocks.caption: The hot key: one key at 20,000 requests per second, 40 percent of all traffic.
rows: Pin the key to a dedicated node pair with consistent hashing, so one bucket sees all of it
a hot node; a topology change

blocks.text: Per-endpoint cost is a multiplier on the tokens taken; tiers are just different policies; neither changes the architecture. Azure's throttling pattern describes the same server-side shape: a service that rejects or degrades when a limit is reached, with autoscaling as the slower complement.

blocks.text: The arithmetic is the L3 point: exactness is a product decision with a price, and at ten times the traffic the price of an exact limiter is the budget of a small team.

L1: A token bucket per key and a shared store.

L2: The local-first design with a correction loop and the latency arithmetic (2,500 decisions per node per second, a few hundred batched store writes per second).
The fail-open argument with its exception (fail closed per policy where a cap is legal or financial).

L3: Whether the product wants a rate limiter, a quota, or both; tiers as policy, not architecture.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements. Ask: who is limited (API key, user, IP, tenant tier)? What limit shape (requests per second with a burst, or per minute)? What happens on reject (429 with a Retry-After header)? Must limits be exact, or is a small overshoot acceptable? Where does it sit (every edge node, or a central service)? State the numbers you will design for and say them aloud: 50k requests per second at the edge across 20 nodes (chosen for the exercise), 1 million distinct keys, decision latency under 1 ms added at p99, limits of the order of 100 requests per second with a burst of 200. Non-goals: billing, abuse detection, DDoS mitigation.

0:05 to 0:10: API and entities. check(key, cost=1) returns allowed, remaining, reset_at; a policy object (key pattern, rate, burst, window, scope); response headers (RateLimit-*, Retry-After, status 429). Say that the limiter is a library plus a shared store, not a separate network hop, because of the latency budget.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design and the diagram. Token bucket per key; local in-process buckets on each node for the fast path; a shared store (Redis-class) for the global count; policies loaded from a config service and cached. Explain the two-tier idea: local buckets take the decision, the shared store corrects them a few times per second.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives. (1) Exactness versus cost: a fixed window per node allows up to N times the limit at window edges; a sliding window approximated from two fixed windows (the Cloudflare method) brings the average rate error to about 6 percent at the cost of two counters per key; an exact distributed token bucket needs an atomic read-modify-write on the shared store per request, which is the 1 ms you do not have at 50k per second across 20 nodes. Choose: local token buckets with a global budget split per node, re-split every 100 ms from the shared counts. (2) Failure modes: shared store down (fail open with local limits, alert; say why fail closed is wrong for a public API and right for a payment endpoint); hot key (one tenant at 40 percent of traffic: a dedicated shard or a local-only limit for that key); node restart (buckets start full; acceptable overshoot of one burst); clock skew (windows keyed on monotonic local time, store time only for TTL).

0:40 to 0:45: Evolution. Tiers and per-endpoint costs (cost parameter), limits per region, moving the policy store to the gateway, metrics: allowed, rejected, overshoot ratio per key, shared-store latency. Ask what the interviewer would like to see deeper. The level shows in the deep dives: L1 gives a correct single-store token bucket; L2 gives the two-tier design with the exactness trade-off and the fail-open argument; L3 asks whether the product needs a limiter at all or a cost-based quota, and reframes the hot tenant as a tenancy question.
Context and scope: The public API, its gateway fleet, the keys and tiers that exist today, and the incidents or abuse that motivate a limiter.
Goals and non-goals: Bound every key within 10 percent per second, add under 1 ms, never make the API unavailable; DDoS and billing out of scope.
Design: This answer fills it: local token buckets, the correction loop against the shared store, the policy service and the header contract.
Alternatives considered: Where the decision is made (shared store per request versus local with correction) and the algorithm choice, with the trade-off table.
Cross-cutting concerns: Observability of drift (allowed, rejected, overshoot ratio per key, store latency) and the fail-open policy as a security review item.
Review questions the doc must answer: The worst-case overshoot under a store outage, and the behaviour when the policy service is down.

sim.heading: Simulate the limiter
sim.caption: The model is one hot key behind one limiter, one API and one database. Read the scale note above the block before comparing its numbers with the exercise.
steps: Raise the offered load to 600 with the limit at 100 and the burst at 200: goodput holds at about 100 requests a second, p99 stays near 78 ms and the API is only about 41% busy.
That is the trade the limiter makes: predictable latency, bought by refusing most of the offered load, about 83% of requests here.

Now raise the limit to 600 and the burst to 400, which is no limit at all: p99 climbs to about 289 ms, the API saturates and about 60% of requests fail, shed by the API instead of refused by the limiter.
